content: 1. Access to maternal and child health services has been explored through a synthesis of qualitative evidence, as documented in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2013 (Issue 10, CD10414.pub2). 2. Ames HMR, Glenton C, and Lewin S conducted a synthesis of qualitative evidence to understand parents’ and informal caregivers’ perspectives and experiences regarding communication about routine childhood vaccinations. This work was published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2017 (Issue 2, CD011787.pub2). 3. Pitchforth E, Lilford RJ, Kebede Y, Asres G, Stanford C, and Frost J performed a pilot study in Gondar, Ethiopia, combining clinical and social science perspectives to assess and understand the quality of care in a labor ward. Their findings were published in Social Science & Medicine in 2010 (Volume 71, Issue 10, Pages 1739–1748). 4. Noyes J and Lewin S authored Chapter 5, which focuses on extracting qualitative evidence, as part of supplementary guidance for including qualitative research in Cochrane systematic reviews of interventions. This guidance was updated in August 2011 and accessed on July 8, 2020. 5. Noyes J and Lewin S also contributed Chapter 6, which provides supplemental guidance on selecting methods for qualitative evidence synthesis and integrating qualitative evidence with Cochrane intervention reviews. This guidance was published by the Cochrane Collaboration Qualitative Methods Group in 2011 and accessed on July 8, 2020. 6. Gopinathan U, Lewin S, and Glenton C synthesized case studies from multiple countries to examine the implementation of large-scale programs aimed at optimizing the health workforce in lowand middle-income settings. Their work was published in Tropical Medicine & International Health in 2014 (Volume 19, Issue 12, Pages 1437–1456). 7. Glenton C, Lewin S, Lawrie TA, Barreix M, Downe S, Finlayson KW, and colleagues discussed the use of qualitative evidence synthesis (QES) to develop implementation considerations and inform implementation processes for guidelines. This was published in Health Research Policy and Systems in 2019 (Volume 17, Article 74). 8. Gough D, Thomas J, and Oliver S clarified differences between review designs and methods in their work published in Systematic Reviews in 2012 (Volume 1, Article 28). 9. Booth A, Noyes J, Fleming K, Gerhardus A, Wahlster P, and van der Wilt GJ provided guidance on selecting qualitative evidence synthesis methods for use in health technology assessments of complex interventions. This guidance was accessed on June 18, 2020. 10. Booth A, Noyes J, Fleming K, Gerhardus A, Wahlster P, and Jan van der Wilt G identified seven RETREAT criteria for selecting qualitative evidence synthesis approaches in their structured methodology review, published in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology in 2018 (Volume 99, Pages 41–52). 11. Toews I, Booth A, Berg RC, Lewin S, Glenton C, Munthe-Kaas HM, and colleagues emphasized the need for further exploration of dissemination bias in qualitative research to facilitate assessment within qualitative evidence syntheses. Their findings were published in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology in 2017 (Volume 88, Pages 133–139). 12. Munthe-Kaas H, Bohren MA, Glenton C, Lewin S, Noyes J, Tunçalp Ö, and colleagues applied GRADE-CERQual to assess methodological limitations in qualitative evidence synthesis findings. This was published in Implementation Science in 2018 (Volume 13, Supplement 1, Article 9). 13. Noyes J, Booth A, Lewin S, Carlsen B, Glenton C, Colvin CJ, and colleagues applied GRADE-CERQual to assess the relevance of data in qualitative evidence synthesis findings. This was published in Implementation Science in 2018 (Volume 13, Supplement 1, Article 4). 14. Colvin CJ, Garside R, Wainwright M, Munthe-Kaas H, Glenton C, Bohren MA, and colleagues applied GRADE-CERQual to assess coherence in qualitative evidence synthesis findings. This was published in Implementation Science in 2018 (Volume 13, Supplement 1, Article 13). 15. Glenton C, Carlsen B, Lewin S, Munthe-Kaas H, Colvin CJ, Tunçalp Ö, and colleagues applied GRADE-CERQual to assess the adequacy of data in qualitative evidence synthesis findings. This was published in Implementation Science in 2018 (Volume 13, Supplement 1, Article 14). 16. Lewin S, Bohren M, Rashidian A, Munthe-Kaas H, Glenton C, Colvin CJ, and colleagues applied GRADE-CERQual to make overall assessments of confidence and create summaries of qualitative findings. This was published in Implementation Science in 2018 (Volume 13, Supplement 1, Article 10). 17. Fleming K, Booth A, Hannes K, Cargo M, and Noyes J provided reporting guidelines for qualitative, implementation, and process evaluation evidence syntheses as part of the Cochrane Qualitative and Implementation Methods Group guidance. This was published in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology in 2018 (Volume 97, Pages 79–85). 18. Tong A, Fleming K, McInnes E, Oliver S, and Craig J developed the ENTREQ framework to enhance transparency in reporting the synthesis of qualitative research. This was published in BMC Medical Research Methodology in 2012 (Volume 12, Article 181). 19. France EF, Cunningham M, Ring N, Uny I, Duncan EAS, Jepson RG, and colleagues improved reporting of meta-ethnography through the eMERGe reporting guidance. This was published in BMC Medical Research Methodology in 2019 (Volume 19, Article 25). 20. Wong G, Greenhalgh T, Westhorp G, Buckingham J, and Pawson R established the RAMESES publication standards for realist syntheses. This was published in BMC Medicine in 2013 (Volume 11, Article 21). 21. Wong G, Greenhalgh T, Westhorp G, Buckingham J, and Pawson R also developed the RAMESES publication standards for meta-narrative reviews. This was published in BMC Medicine in 2013 (Volume 11, Article 20). 22. Booth A proposed the STARLITE framework to standardize the reporting of literature searches. This was published in the Journal of the Medical Library Association in 2006 (Volume 94, Issue 4, Pages 421–429). 23. The World Health Organization (WHO) is a specialized agency of the United Nations, established in 1948, with the primary responsibility for international health matters and public health. The WHO Regional Office for Europe is one of six regional offices worldwide, each tailored to address the specific health conditions of the countries it serves.
